BGP and ASN Lookup

Enter an ASN, IP address or prefix to see who originates it, which prefixes an AS announces, its neighbours in AS paths, and RPKI origin validation.

Try:

What this BGP looking glass shows

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how networks on the internet tell each other which IP prefixes they can reach. Each network is an Autonomous System identified by an ASN. This tool queries the public RIPEstat data API, which is built from RIPE RIS route collectors around the world, so you see routing as observed from the global table.

Looking up an ASN

For an ASN you get the registered holder, whether it originates prefixes that are visible globally, how many IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes it announces, and the neighbours seen next to it in AS paths. Click any neighbour or prefix to pivot to it.

Looking up an IP address or prefix

For an IP or prefix you get the covering announced prefix, the origin ASN or ASNs, the registry block it belongs to, and an RPKI validation result for each origin.

Understanding RPKI status

  • Valid: a ROA authorises this origin AS to announce this prefix at this length.
  • Invalid (wrong origin ASN): a ROA covers the prefix but names a different AS. This can indicate a hijack or a misconfiguration.
  • Invalid (too specific): the announced prefix is longer than the ROA's maximum length.
  • Not found: no ROA covers the announcement. Many prefixes still have none.

Frequently asked questions

What is an ASN?

An Autonomous System Number identifies a network under a single routing policy, such as an ISP, a cloud provider or a large enterprise. ASNs are assigned by regional registries like RIPE NCC, ARIN and APNIC.

Why does an AS show as not originating prefixes?

Some ASNs only provide transit, carrying traffic for others, and do not originate prefixes of their own. Others originate prefixes that too few route collectors see to count as globally visible.

Why might a prefix show as not announced?

It may be unused, announced only within a private network, filtered by most upstreams, or announced as part of a larger covering prefix.

Where does the data come from?

All data is fetched live from RIPEstat by your browser. It reflects what RIPE's route collectors currently see and can differ slightly from other looking glasses.

Can I use this to troubleshoot an outage?

It is a quick first check: confirm a prefix is still announced, see which ASN originates it and whether RPKI validates. For real-time path analysis use your provider's looking glass or a collector with live updates.
